coachMessages.text: Gray has three discs in a row with one empty square to complete the four. What is Green's only safe move?

slides.infoProse: When your opponent can complete four-in-a-row on their very next move, you must block that square. There is no better move — building your own position while your opponent wins is not strategy, it is a loss.

coachMessages.text: You built — but Gray didn't wait. See what happens when Green ignores the threat.

slides.infoProse: This is the consequence of building instead of blocking: your opponent completes four-in-a-row on the very next turn. No matter how promising your own move looked, the game is over before you get to use it. Block first, always.

coachMessages.text: Threats don't only run sideways. A vertical or diagonal three-in-a-row is just as urgent — the same rule applies.

legendItems.label: Green is building here (not yet a threat)

slides.infoProse: The direction doesn't change the urgency. A vertical stack, a diagonal, a horizontal run — all are equally immediate threats. The rule is the same in every case: one empty square completes the four, and the block is forced. Here Gray's diagonal three must be blocked at the bottom of the first column right away — Green's own diagonal is still two squares short, so building it does not answer an immediate threat.

coachMessages.text: Gray has three in a row — but is the completing square actually reachable this turn? Look carefully before blocking.

legendItems.label: Green can even win right now — the buried threat changes nothing

slides.infoProse:
Not every three-in-a-row is an immediate threat. If the completing square is buried — sitting above empty cells in its column — Gray cannot reach it this turn, so Green does not need to spend a move blocking it. Always check: is that square the very next disc that can be placed in its column? If not, the threat is not yet immediate. Here the check pays off at once: instead of blocking a threat that isn't real yet, Green is free to play the strongest move on the board — and in the second column Green can even win immediately.

Can you spot another similar case on this board for Gray?

socratic._boardInstructions: Show a minimal board where Red has three horizontal discs across the bottom of columns 0, 1, and 2 (row 0), leaving column 3 row 0 as the only empty cell that completes Red's four-in-a-row — it is immediately playable since nothing is below it. Yellow has two discs at row 0 in columns 5 and 6, making column 4 look like a tempting building move. Mark Red's completing cell at col 3 row 0 with 'tg' (this is the mandatory block) and the tempting Yellow building cell at col 4 row 0 with 'td' (the trap — playing here hands Red the win). No other overlays are needed. The student must choose col 3 to block Red's immediate threat rather than extend their own position.

ask.text: I'm going to make a mistake here. See if you can punish it.
ask.text_es: Voy a cometer un error aquí. Mirá si podés castigarlo.

wrong1.text: Not quite — look for the right square. Try again.
wrong1.text_es: No exactamente — buscá la casilla correcta. Intentalo de nuevo.

hint.text: Look for an even square directly above one of my discs.
hint.text_es: Buscá una casilla par justo encima de una de mis fichas.
